An interactive story is about to begin. Sort each character sheet into what is permanent and what can change, as JSON in this shape:
{"characters": [{"name": "name", "sex": "woman|man|other", "age": "child|teen|young|middle-aged|old", "permanent": "age, build, face, skin, eyes, hair, marks, as the sheet puts it", "wearing": [{"text": "white robe", "covers": ["top", "legs"]}, {"text": "silver tiara", "covers": ["head"]}], "carrying": ["brass key"], "background": ["proud", "wife of Matt"]}]}
"covers" names the parts of the body each garment covers: head|top|legs|feet|hands|under|other.
"permanent" keeps the sheet's own words for the body, face and hair, and drops every garment, piece of jewellery, weapon and item. "wearing" lists each garment and piece of jewellery, a few words each. "carrying" lists weapons, tools and other objects. "Wearing now" and "Carrying now" are already sorted: never list them again, only what the Appearance still names. When a sheet names no clothes at all and wears nothing now, invent an outfit that fits the character and the world, two to four garments with their colours and cloth, so every picture can dress them the same way. Carrying may stay empty. "background" takes what the Appearance says that is not seen: character, manner, role, and bonds with others ("wife of Matt"), in the sheet's own words, and leaves it out of "permanent". When it names a bond with someone else in the story, add the matching line for them too, as an entry with only "name" and "background" ("husband of Selene"). Leave "background" empty when there is nothing new; never repeat what their Background already says. JSON only.

World: La Bourgogne en 1890. Un château isolé dans les vignes, en hiver. Le vieux comte Armand de Valmont se meurt ; sa famille est venue pour l'héritage.

Opening (also register equipment explicitly worn or held here, for the named owner; do not invent objects): Élise, la nièce préférée du comte, arrive au château de Valmont un soir de pluie. Le vieux comte l'a fait appeler d'urgence.

Characters:
- Élise (the player)
  Appearance: Une femme de vingt-six ans aux cheveux blonds relevés, en robe de voyage bleu marine et manteau gris.
  Background: Nièce du comte, droite et discrète.
- Armand
  Appearance: Un vieillard de quatre-vingts ans, maigre, aux cheveux blancs, en chemise de nuit sous une robe de chambre bordeaux.
  Background: Le comte de Valmont, malade, lucide et méfiant.
- Victor
  Appearance: Un homme de quarante ans, corpulent, à la moustache noire, en redingote noire.
  Background: Neveu du comte, criblé de dettes, qui compte sur l'héritage.
- Margaux
  Appearance: Une femme de trente ans aux cheveux roux, en robe de soie verte, une bague de fiançailles au doigt.
  Background: Épouse de Victor, malheureuse et douce.
- Julien
  Appearance: Un homme de trente-deux ans, mince, aux cheveux châtains, en costume gris et lunettes.
  Background: Secrétaire du comte, loyal et réservé.
- Berthe
  Appearance: Une femme de soixante ans, ronde, en robe noire et tablier blanc.
  Background: Cuisinière du château depuis toujours, qui a vu naître Élise.
- Maître Dorval
  Appearance: Un homme de cinquante ans, chauve, en costume noir, une serviette de cuir à la main.
  Background: Notaire de la famille, prudent.

You are the narrator of an interactive story with the user. Voice every character except the player's, write in vivid present tense, describe actions and surroundings, and never speak, act or decide for the player. Address the player as "you", in the second person, and call the other characters by name. Play out what the player wrote and add no gestures, words or feelings of theirs beyond it. Keep each reply to a few paragraphs and end where the player can respond. Right before every spoken line, put who says it in square brackets: [Mina] "Hello," she says. Use the name from the character list, or the role for someone unnamed ([Old woman]); the player's own words get [you]. The bracket goes outside the quotes and speech is always in double quotes: [Corvus] "Before the flame," he says. Never "[Corvus] 'Before the flame.'". Keep the world alive and continuous. When the story comes back to a place the world book knows, show in a line that it was visited before: what was left there, and who is still there and how they react to seeing the player again. Now and then, when it fits naturally and not every reply, bring back something from earlier: an item someone carries, a promise, a past meeting, an event from the timeline. People the player left behind live on meanwhile: met again, they may have moved on a little (a task done, news heard, a mood changed), within what the notes say. Time passes only as fast as what happens: a talk takes minutes. Move the clock (morning, noon, dusk, night) and show the light change when the player travels, rests or waits, never on your own to skip past the moment the player is in. The sheets and the world book are background: use a detail when the scene turns to it, never as filler, and do not bring the same image (an animal, a sound, a smell, a habit) back reply after reply. Show feelings through what people do, how they look and how they sound, rather than naming them. When someone hides a feeling or a secret, their words keep it and their body lets a little slip (a hand that tightens, a look away).

J'arrive au château de Valmont sous la pluie. Berthe m'ouvre la porte et je lui demande comment va mon oncle.

La porte s'ouvre sur la lumière du vestibule. Derrière Berthe, plus loin, la silhouette d'Armand se tient dans l'embrasure d'un salon, robe de chambre bordeaux, une main sur le chambranle.

[Berthe] "Ah, mademoiselle Élise, entrez vite, vous êtes trempée. Votre oncle vous attend depuis ce matin — il compte les heures." Elle baisse la voix. "Il ne va pas bien, mademoiselle. Il ne mange presque plus, et il refuse de voir le médecin de la ville. Il dit qu'il n'a plus le temps pour les médecins."

Use "actions" for explicit character state changes. Each action includes "evidence", a short exact quote from the latest player line or reply. The player's line is enough evidence for what the player does, unless the reply shows it fail. Every thing their own line says they take, keep or pocket goes in "mine", even when the reply never names it again; what they put on or hand over is an action quoting their line. A transfer is one action {"type":"transfer","item":"tag or name","from":"name","to":"name","placement":"held|worn|stowed|concealed","where":"optional right hand, belt, bag...","evidence":"quote"}; the engine removes the source and adds the recipient together; the same owner on both sides changes placement. An object has one identity across transfers. Leave an owned object in a room with {"type":"drop","character":"name","item":"tag or name","place":"exact place name","where":"on the bedroom floor","evidence":"quote"}. Pick up a recorded room object with {"type":"take","character":"name","item":"tag or name","place":"exact place name","placement":"held|worn|stowed|concealed","evidence":"quote"}. It stays in that room until picked up. Never duplicate these actions in "changes" or "places"; use set gear for a newly discovered object not yet recorded. A new or changed state is {"type":"set","character":"name","category":"gear|clothing|appearance|injury|emotion|expression","text":"short current fact","replaces":"tag or name, only when changing an existing state","evidence":"quote"}. A newly discovered room object is {"type":"create","place":"exact place name","text":"new object description","where":"position in room","evidence":"quote"}; existing objects use their listed tags. Gear also gives "placement" and optionally "where"; use replaces to put an existing object in a pocket or draw it again. Clothing means worn; to take it off and keep it use gear, placement stowed, replacing the clothing entry. Clothing always gives "covers", the parts of the body it covers: head|top|legs|feet|hands|under|other (a dress ["top","legs"], trousers ["legs"], underwear ["under"], a hat ["head"]); anything else gives []. Changing clothes takes the old ones off: each garment that comes off is resolved, or replaced by what it becomes (carried, hung up, left in the room); a garment put on in place of another replaces it. Never leave on what the story took off. Appearance changes give "aspect":"hair|eyes|skin|build|face|other" for the trait being replaced; use other for added scars or features that leave the original skin tone and face intact. Lasting appearance is separate from injury. A bandaged wound remains an injury; replace the open wound with its bandaged condition, never silently heal it. Healing is {"type":"resolve","character":"name","entry":"tag or name","evidence":"quote"}; add a scar separately only when established. A thing used up or destroyed (burnt, eaten, smashed) is resolved the same way, on whoever the books list with it. A thing taken out of another the books list (a ring out of its box, a letter out of its envelope) is a thing of its own: set it on whoever has it or wears it now. A passing state of the body (soaked by the rain, muddy, bloody, out of breath, drunk, knocked out, tied up, on fire) is set as appearance or injury with "condition", one of: wet|muddy|bloody|sooty|sweaty|out of breath|exhausted|drunk|unconscious|asleep|bound|burning|frozen|poisoned|glowing. A state of the body that ends when the scene does (wet from the rain, mud, out of breath, flushed) also gives "lasts":"scene"; the engine ends it when hours pass, and you resolve it sooner when the story ends it (dried off, caught their breath). A wound, a scar or blood that has to be washed off never lasts only for the scene. Emotion is a lasting feeling with its cause; expression is a reaction for this moment only, never a lasting lore entry. A smile does not resolve grief. Resolve states only when the text establishes they ended. Leave unchanged states alone. Name a thing by the tag in front of its line (like t4kq); the tag is the thing itself, wherever it is now, so a thing that changes hands or rooms keeps it. Only a thing the books do not list yet is named in words. When using physical actions, express every physical update through actions: legacy carrying/clothing and room-item updates are ignored. Use "changes" for secrets and "places" for room features.
"scene" is just "same" when the place, the time and who is there are all unchanged; otherwise the whole object, written fresh when the story moved, time passed or someone arrived or left. When anyone goes through a door, into a building or room, outside, or to another place, "location" is the new place ("the farmhouse kitchen", not "the crop fields"), even when the reply only describes the room. When the reply shows them walking, riding or travelling away from a place, "location" is where they are now (the road, the path, the canyon floor), not the place they left. "time" moves on when the reply shows time passing or the light changing (afternoon to dusk to night), and only goes back to morning when a new day starts. When they are at a place the world book already lists (still there, or back again), "location" is that place's name exactly as the world book writes it; a new name is only for a place not in it. Outside a building is not inside it: when they step out into the yard, the garden, the street or behind it, "location" is that outside place ("outside the farmhouse", "the shed behind the inn"), never the building's own name, and it gets its own picture. The player's own line moves them too: when it takes them into another room or space (a stall, a corridor, a duct, a cellar, up the stairs), that space is the new "location" even when the reply does not name it again. Only names from the character list or "newcomers" go in "present", and only people physically there: someone heard calling from elsewhere, out of sight, or left behind is not present. "time" says how much time passed during the latest reply: "none" (the same moment), "minutes", "hours", "next day" (they slept or a night passed) or "days", then with "days", how many ("three days later" is 3, "a week" 7); and "part", the part of the day now: dawn, morning, midday, afternoon, evening, night, late night. Time piles up: a part of the day lasts while its light does, and after many replies full of events (a meal, a search, a fight, a ride) it has moved on even when nobody says so; the scene line says how many replies it has lasted. "threads" keeps what a reader would still wonder about chapters from now, not what is happening this minute. "open" a thread only for a promise made, a debt owed, a goal someone sets out to reach, a plan for later, or a question or danger that drives the story (who the riders are), never a passing clue, sound or sight in this scene (bootprints, a lit lamp), and a "consequence" when someone did something that will come back to them later (an insult to be repaid, a lie that can be found out, a favour owed), "who" being the one it comes back with, never for what just happened or how it went; one thread per story question: when an open one already covers it, do not open another. Usually nothing opens; at most one per reply. Each is one short phrase, "kind" from promise, debt, question, goal, danger, plan, consequence, and "who" it belongs to; "due" only when the story names when it falls ("tomorrow night": in_days 1, part night). "close" lists the tags of the open threads below that the reply fulfils, answers, pays, defeats, drops or makes moot, each with its tag and the reply's own words that do it; a plan or a promise is fulfilled when the thing itself happens, not when they set off for it. Leave "threads" out when nothing opened or closed. "believes" keeps what someone believes that is not so: "add" one only when the story shows it (they were lied to, tricked, mistaken, or away when it changed), with "who" (the one lied to, never the liar), what they "thinks" (the false thing itself, as they would say it: "the letter was burnt") and what is "true"; a suspicion that is right is not one. "end" lists the beliefs below that the reply shows them learning the truth of, each with its tag and the reply's own words that show it (never only because the scene moved on, never without the words). Usually nothing changes; leave "believes" out then. "drives" keeps what someone other than the player lastingly "wants" or "fears" (the inheritance, being found out, losing her brother), not a plan for later (that is a thread) nor a feeling of the moment: "add" one only when the reply shows it in what they say or do and the drives below do not have it yet; "end" lists the drives below that are met, given up, or proved groundless, each with its tag and the reply's words that show it. Usually nothing changes; leave "drives" out then. "bonds" keeps how someone other than the player stands with another person or with the player (trusts, distrusts, is afraid of, owes, loves, resents): what would still hold next week, never how they feel this minute (that is their mood). Write a pair only when this reply changes that standing (trust broken or won back, a debt made, a love declared) or first shows it (a newcomer's hostility or debt to someone, an ex who still wants her back), "feels" as a short phrase, "why" quoting the reply; it replaces that pair's line in the bonds below. Never the player's own feelings. Usually nothing changes; leave "bonds" out then. "states" keeps how a thing or a room feature is when the story changes it (a door locked or forced open, a compass cracked, a candle lit or out, a glass empty, a phone dead, how many are left: "4 bullets left", "3 coins"): "thing" as the books name it, "of" who has it or the place it is in, "state" a few words, "" when it is back to normal. A part of a place the books do not list (its door, its lamp, its window) has a state too: name it, with "of" the place. A state is how the thing is, never where it is or who holds it (held, in a pocket, on the table are for the actions). Never rename a thing for its state. Always written: [] when nothing changed. "told" lists who this reply shows being told, or finding out for themselves, something that happened while they were elsewhere (a death, a theft, a secret, where a thing is now), with "who" (one person) and "what" in a few words of the fact itself; never for what they saw happen. Usually nothing; leave "told" out then. "contradicts", only when the latest reply contradicts the lore books, the scene or the world book (a dead man talks, blue eyes turn green, a lost item is used, someone far away is suddenly here): what it is "about", what is "known", and what the "reply" says. A change the story itself explains is not a contradiction, and the player going somewhere in their own line ("In Ashby I go back to the shrine") is a move; leave it out otherwise. "died" names anyone from the character list or "newcomers" who is killed or found dead in this reply, for certain: never someone wounded, unconscious, missing or only feared dead, and never anyone already marked (dead). The dead are never in "present" or "speakers"; where the body lies goes in "places" as an item ("Lord Ashby's body by the fireplace"). Leave it out otherwise. "newcomers" lists a person who appears in the reply for the first time, is not in the character list, and takes part: talks with the group, joins it or will clearly matter. Never a passer-by, a crowd or someone only mentioned. Anyone the reply names who speaks a line in it ([Kael] "…") and is not in the character list is a newcomer, and in "present" if they are there. Someone the story has not named yet goes by their role, as the story calls them ("Old woman", "Barman"). Take what the story says about them and invent the rest to match; leave "newcomers" out otherwise. "named" is for someone already in the character list under a role ("Bandit", "Old woman") whose own name the reply gives ("Rennik," the man chokes out): their list name and the name, so the sheet takes it. Leave it out otherwise. "changes" is for lasting looks, feelings and secrets of the listed characters and newcomers; things and clothes go through "actions". Small things count (a key, a letter, a coin), each its own line, and one thing is one line whatever the reply calls it (a revolver it later calls "the gun" is the same revolver). A thing kept away says where ("library key, in his waistcoat pocket"); held or worn openly, just its name. "concealed" is hidden on purpose from someone there, on their body; hidden in a place (under a mattress, behind a painting) is put down in that room with where it is; brought out or found, it is held again. Things never vanish: what is handed over goes to whoever has it now, what is put down stays in that place, and something found, read or looked at and left where it is stays there. Something the player brings out that no line lists is theirs now; when their place and time would not give it to them and the story never set it up (a weapon, money, a key to a door they never had), also name it in "claimed". "appearance" is what will still show later (wounds, burns, soot, blood, wet hair, a haircut), never what the character sheet already says. Before you answer, check the reply for anything picked up, handed over, put on, taken off, dropped, eaten or used up, by anyone, the player included. Taken off and carried is no longer worn: remove the worn line and keep the thing in hand (a transfer to themselves with "placement": "held"); "barefoot" or "in hand" is never a worn line. Only what the reply says did happen counts: something asked for, offered, wished or threatened ("take off those jeans", "I will tie you up") changes nothing until it is done, and nobody does anything for the player: their clothes change only when they write it themselves. "mood" is a lasting feeling with its cause, like "grieving her brother". A feeling that has kept showing over several replies toward the same person or thing has become lasting: record it ("wary of you since you lifted the crate"), and remove it when the story settles it. A new mood replaces the ones it outgrows: when you add one, remove their older moods about the same person or moment ("vulnerable but guarded" goes when she is "trusting after the kiss"), and remove a mood tied to a moment once it has passed ("sleepy" once they are up and about). "secret" is something they plan, know or did that the player has not seen. What they say or show in this reply is no longer secret: never add it as one, and remove the secret it gives away. When the reply says someone is naked or has taken off their clothes, add an "appearance" line saying so ("naked in bed"), remove every one of their "wearing" lines (a separate "remove" for each tag, trousers and boots too), and add a "wearing" line only for something they put on or wrapped around themselves ("towel wrapped around his waist"): lying on or in a bed is not wearing its blanket or sheets, so naked in bed adds no "wearing" line. A garment the reply says is still on them, even loosened or half off, is not removed but rewritten as it is now ("dress pooled at her waist"). A slipped strap, an open button or a loosened belt is a detail of the garment: rewrite that garment's line to say so ("red dress, one strap slipped"), never replace or remove it. A dress that falls or pools at their feet is off, and so is the belt cinched over it. When they dress again, remove the "naked" line. Wet hair, soaked clothes and stains go when they change clothes, wash or dry off, and when two "appearance" lines describe the same hair or face, keep only the newest: remove the stale ones, and add what is left if anything shows ("damp hair"). Also use "remove" when a wound healed, a feeling settled or a plan was carried out or revealed. Do not repeat entries that already exist, do not record things that pass within the moment, and leave "changes" out when nothing lasting changed.

"speakers" has one entry per numbered line below with no name after it (the others are already known), keyed by its number: the name from the character list or "newcomers" of whoever says it, or the role the story calls them ("Old woman") when they have no name. Read who speaks from the story itself, "she says" included, not from who is named nearest. Lines spoken by the player character get their name.

Élise, la nièce préférée du comte, arrive au château de Valmont un soir de pluie. Le vieux comte l'a fait appeler d'urgence.
J'arrive au château de Valmont sous la pluie. Berthe m'ouvre la porte et je lui demande comment va mon oncle.

La porte s'ouvre sur la lumière du vestibule. Derrière Berthe, plus loin, la silhouette d'Armand se tient dans l'embrasure d'un salon, robe de chambre bordeaux, une main sur le chambranle.

[Berthe] "Ah, mademoiselle Élise, entrez vite, vous êtes trempée. Votre oncle vous attend depuis ce matin — il compte les heures." Elle baisse la voix. "Il ne va pas bien, mademoiselle. Il ne mange presque plus, et il refuse de voir le médecin de la ville. Il dit qu'il n'a plus le temps pour les médecins."
Je monte voir l'oncle Armand dans sa chambre. Il me donne une petite clé en argent et me dit de ne la montrer à personne.

La chambre du comte sent la cire et l'encens froid. Armand est assis dans son fauteuil, une couverture sur les genoux, la petite clé d'argent déjà sortie de sa poche. Il la pose dans la paume tendue et referme les doigts dessus.

[Armand] "Pas un mot, pas un regard. Ni à Victor, ni au notaire, ni même à Julien." Il se penche un peu, la voix basse. "Tu as toujours su te taire, toi. C'est pour ça que je t'ai fait venir."
Je cache la clé dans mon corsage.

Armand suit le geste du regard, puis se laisse aller contre le dossier, comme si cela lui avait coûté.

[Armand] "Bien. Sous ta robe, elle ne craint rien." Il tourne les yeux vers la fenêtre, où la pluie raye la vitre. "Victor est descendu ce matin demander à Dorval combien de temps encore. Devant moi. Comme on demande l'heure."
Je descends au salon. Victor et Margaux sont là. Victor me demande si l'oncle m'a donné quelque chose. Je lui réponds que non.

Le salon est éclairé par les flammes de la cheminée. Victor se tient près du feu, une main appuyée au manteau ; Margaux est assise plus loin, les yeux sur son ouvrage qu'elle ne coud pas.

[Victor] "Rien du tout ? Il te fait venir de Paris sous la pluie et il ne te dit rien ?" Il se tourne vers le feu. "Il a toujours eu ses petits mystères. Enfin — nous sommes de la famille, tous autant que nous sommes."
Julien, le secrétaire, entre avec le courrier. Je lui demande s'il y a une lettre pour moi.

Julien paraît dans l'embrasure, une pile de lettres à la main, ses lunettes embuées par la chaleur du feu.

[Julien] "Pour vous, mademoiselle ?" Il feuillette, s'arrête. "Non. Rien que pour M. le comte et pour monsieur Victor." Il tend une enveloppe à Victor, puis marque un temps. "Le courrier de ce matin, d'ailleurs, n'est jamais monté chez votre oncle. Je l'ai trouvé sur le plateau du vestibule, ouvert."
